title: Not my judgment
hookLine: the tyrant has power over the body, never the judgment (Discourses 1.19)

lines: NOW HE WORKS FOR THE EMPEROR.
cards: Epictetus' old master, Epaphroditus, once sold a slave who made shoes, because he thought the man was useless. Then someone in the emperor's household bought the shoemaker, and he became the emperor's own shoemaker.
Suddenly Epaphroditus couldn't do enough for him. How is our dear Felicio, he'd ask. Come looking for Epaphroditus, and you'd be told he was in a meeting with Felicio.
Epictetus tells it with a straight face, and lets it sit.

teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter nineteen: how we should behave toward tyrants. Felicio is the joke that opens the door. Why did Epaphroditus suddenly fawn over his old shoemaker?
Not because Felicio changed, but because Felicio was now near the emperor. Then the real question. What frightens people?
The tyrant and his guards? No. Nothing that is free by nature can be troubled by anything but itself.
What troubles us is our own judgments.

teach.h: THE TYRANT CAN'T REACH THE WILL.
teach.b: So when the tyrant says, I'll chain your leg, the person who prizes the leg begs for mercy. The person who prizes their own will says: if it seems better to you, chain it. Take the body, if you have power over it.
But no one, Epictetus says, has power over another person's will. They can threaten, and make choosing costly, but the choosing stays with you.
Tyrants come in small sizes, too: a boss who controls your schedule, a relative who controls the family's approval, an online crowd that controls how you feel about yourself.
The question works on all of them: what exactly can they touch? Your paycheck, maybe. Your mood, only if you hand it over.
Your judgment, never. That's not a promise that standing firm will be painless. It's a map of where the fight actually is.

how: Some Stoic readers sort a fear into what it could touch and what it can't, keeping their attention on their own judgment and choices.

o: a rigid rule that nobody is allowed to question
a judgment, the settled view that shapes how you react
a tyrant's order that has to be obeyed at once

games.q: not my judgment: tap the pairs.

s: Felicio changed, so Epaphroditus respected him more
Felicio didn't change; he was simply near power now.
Epictetus says the tyrant and his guards are what really frighten us
he says it's our own judgments; nothing free by nature is troubled except by itself.
Epaphroditus was his master before he was freed.

games.q: the tyrant says: I'll chain you and take your property. you're a student of Epictetus. what's your answer?
o: if it seems better to you, chain me; my will you can't touch.
games.why: the student lets the tyrant have what was never fully his, and keeps the one thing no one has power over: the will.

practice: Name one fear that's been pressing on you lately: losing a job, someone's disapproval, a diagnosis, money.
Sort it, first what it could touch, my income, my plans, my comfort, my body, then what it can't: what I value, how I treat people, whether I stay honest. Rest your attention on that second list.

wordCard.voice: Dogma. Greek for judgment, a settled opinion: Epictetus' word for the views that shape our reactions, which no tyrant can touch.

orig.note: Greek dogma: a judgment or settled opinion; Epictetus uses it for the views that shape our reactions.

carryVoice: Your line: the choosing stays with you. They can make it costly; they can't make it for you. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.19 (how we should behave toward tyrants; Felicio)
